item.title: Report urges 'policy reset' for Canada's telecom sector to help operators invest
item.description: A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions to invest.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions for companies to invest in their networks at a time when traditional revenues are plateauing and capital costs are on the rise. The paper from U.K.-based Global System for Mobile Communications calls for a “policy reset” that prioritizes affordable and predictable spectrum pricing, support for 5G and AI infrastructure such as data centres, and improved regulatory certainty. It says mobile technologies and services generated 5.4 per cent of Canada’s GDP last year, or roughly $120 billion of economic value — a figure expected to rise to $170 billion by 2030, thanks to growing adoption of technologies such as 5G, Internet of Things and AI. In recent years, the CRTC has introduced various measures aimed at boosting cellphone and internet competition in Canada, empowering consumers, and lowering costs. But without a policy shift, the report warns that network quality and innovation could gradually weaken. It points to challenges facing telecom operators in Canada such as fewer new subscribers because of slower immigration, flat revenues and the rising cost of spectrum licences. The Global System for Mobile Communications is an organization representing mobile operators worldwide. This is its first Canadian policy report. --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

item.title: Trump and Vance to announce a US$25M whistleblower program to encourage public to report alleged fraud
item.description: The Trump administration is set to announce a US$25 million program to encourage the public to blow the whistle on suspected fraud in the federal government.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Vice President JD Vance are set Tuesday to announce a US$25 million program to encourage the public to blow the whistle on suspected fraud in the federal government as they ramp up an existing effort to end the abuse of federal programs and dollars. Under the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, or WHIP, anyone who submits a tip to fraud.gov that leads to a fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action is eligible to receive up to US$30,000, the White House said. The Justice Department will administer the program. The Republican president has undertaken an aggressive effort to eliminate fraud throughout the government. Trump established a task force on the topic in March and put Vance in charge of it. They are scheduled to announce the fund during a joint appearance in the Oval Office later Tuesday. “Every day, President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud is zeroing in on the rampant abuse of taxpayer dollars and giving Americans the accountability they deserve. This administration has zero tolerance for individuals who steal from Americans,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis. During the Oval Office event, Trump will present a US$10,000 check to Nick Shirley, a right-wing influencer who posted a video last year that said members of Minnesota’s Somali community were running fake childcare centers to collect federal subsidies. The video caught the attention of the Trump administration and conservative activists, though inspectors said the centers were operating as expected. Investigations, searches and arrests followed. In July, one woman, Fahima Mahamud, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States by submitting inflated reimbursement claims for meals allegedly served to children at her childcare center, according to the Justice Department. The White House says Mahamud was featured in Shirley’s video. --- Darlene Superville, The Associated Press

item.title: GM shares sink as full-year profit forecast misses Wall Street estimates
item.description: General Motors’ third-quarter core profit rose sharply on the back of strong pickup truck sales, but its shares fell on Tuesday after the automaker’s earnings-per-share forecast for the full year fell ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: General Motors’ third-quarter core profit rose sharply on the back of strong pickup truck sales, but its shares fell on Tuesday after the automaker’s earnings-per-share forecast for the full year fell short of analyst expectations. The company said quarterly earnings before interest and tax, not including one-time items (adjusted EBIT), rose 22 per cent from a year earlier, to US per cent4.1 billion. That amounted to per cent3.70 per share, topping analyst expectations of per cent3.63, according to LSEG data. GM said it expected to end 2026 with adjusted EBIT in the range of per cent14.5 billion to per cent15.5 billion, narrowed from previous guidance of per cent14 billion to per cent16 billion. It tightened its annual adjusted earnings-per-share forecast to between per cent12.75 and per cent13.75, the midpoint of which is below analysts’ estimates of per cent13.41, according to data compiled by LSEG. GM shares fell about four per cent in premarket trading. Confidence in ‘27 GM said it remained confident despite inflationary pressures from higher logistics and energy costs, tariffs and other expenses. Commodity inflation, including higher expenses for logistics and computer chips, would total about per cent2 billion this year, the high end of its previous forecast, it said. Its board approved a multi-year, per cent20 billion stock buyback program. GM has bought back about per cent29.5 billion of its own shares since 2023, driving down its overall share count to help its per-share profit results. In the third quarter, it sold a higher mix of large pickup trucks and fewer electric vehicles, which helped the bottom line. The company has been pulling back on sales of EVs, which historically have lost money, following the Trump administration’s withdrawal of support for them. Revenue totaled per cent50 billion, up 2.9 per cent from a year earlier. In North America, the profit margin improved to 8.7 per cent, from 6.2 per cent a year earlier, despite a slight decline in quarterly sales. GM said “the path forward is more challenging,” but reiterated that it expects next year’s results to be better, assuming continued strong consumer demand and a moderating of cost pressures on commodities and logistics. (Reporting by Kalea Hall; Editing by Mike Colias, Kirsten Donovan and Joe Bavier)
